procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 19, 1968 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 72 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Patna High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 72 of 1966 and issued a judgment and order on July 19, 1968. The outcome of the appeal in the High Court is not explicitly stated, but it is implied that the High Court upheld the conviction and sentence from the trial court, as the defendant is appealing to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by special leave to appeal the Patna High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that it ordinarily does not reappreciate evidence unless exceptional circumstances exist, and that the appellant cannot raise points at the final hearing that were not fit to be urged at the preliminary stage when leave to appeal was requested.

directions: The appellants are on bail. They shall now surrender to the authorities and undergo the remaining portion of the sentence imposed on them.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution, should reappreciate evidence in the absence of exceptional circumstances or grave injustice.

facts: The case was an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution against a criminal conviction.
The appellants' conviction was based on the testimony of a single injured witness (P.W. 9), as the High Court had disbelieved other witnesses who were meant to corroborate his account.
Both the trial court and the High Court had accepted the testimony of the injured witness as credible.
law: The Supreme Court ordinarily does not reappreciate evidence in an appeal by special leave under Article 136.
An exception to this rule is made only when there are "exceptional and special circumstances" showing that a "substantial and grave injustice has been done."
Such circumstances arise from a "serious misappreciation of the evidence" by the lower courts (the trial court and the High Court).
Citing the precedent of *Hem Raj v. The State of Ajmer*, the Court affirmed that the grant of special leave does not entitle an appellant to reopen the entire case and contest all findings of fact.
application: The Court first established the legal principle that it does not act as a regular court of appeal to re-evaluate evidence.
It then examined the case to see if any exceptional circumstances or grave injustice existed that would warrant its intervention.
The Court found that the concurrent findings of the trial court and the High Court, which both found the testimony of the injured witness (P.W. 9) to be reliable, were well-founded.
It concluded that there was no serious misappreciation of evidence by the lower courts and therefore, no reason for the Supreme Court to differ from their conclusions.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the plea to reappreciate the evidence, holding that its strict standard for intervention was not met. It ruled that it will not interfere with concurrent findings of fact from lower courts in an appeal under Article 136 unless there are exceptional circumstances or a grave injustice, neither of which was found in this case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants was justified when it was based on the sole testimony of a single witness (P.W. 9), especially after the High Court had disbelieved other corroborating witnesses.

facts: P.W. 9 was the sole witness to the attack on himself, as the High Court had disbelieved the other witnesses who tried to corroborate his story.
The incident occurred in daylight, and P.W. 9 knew the appellants well, so there was no difficulty in identifying them.
P.W. 9 had no motive to falsely implicate the appellants.
He named the appellants as his assailants at the earliest opportunity (in his dying declaration).
Medical evidence, including the nature of his serious injuries, corroborated his version of the attack.
Both the trial court and the High Court had previously accepted P.W. 9's testimony as credible.
law: The testimony of a single witness can be sufficient for a conviction if it is found to be credible and reliable.
Minor contradictions or embellishments in a witness's statement do not necessarily detract from the overall value and truthfulness of their testimony.
The fact that other corroborating witnesses are disbelieved does not automatically invalidate the testimony of a primary, credible witness.
application: The Supreme Court found P.W. 9's testimony to be highly credible on its own merits. The circumstances of the attack (daylight, prior acquaintance with assailants) made his identification reliable.
The Court considered the corroboration from the medical evidence to be a significant factor in establishing the truth of his account.

The Court dismissed the contradictions in P.W. 9's statements (e.g., the exact type of weapon used, an exaggeration about other attackers) as being of "very minor significance" and insufficient to discredit his core testimony.
The Court explicitly stated that the High Court's decision to disbelieve the other two witnesses did not "throw any doubt on the testimony of P.W. 9."

The Court gave weight to the fact that two lower courts (the trial court and the High Court) had already concurrently found P.W. 9's testimony to be substantially true, and it saw no reason to differ from their conclusion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the conviction was justified. It held that the testimony of the single witness, P.W. 9, was credible, reliable, and strong enough to stand on its own. His account was supported by medical evidence and the surrounding circumstances, and the minor contradictions in his statements were not significant enough to undermine his testimony. Therefore, the fact that other corroborating witnesses had been disbelieved by the High Court did not invalidate the conviction based on his sole evidence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution, should reappreciate evidence in the absence of exceptional circumstances or grave injustice.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued for the reappreciation of evidence, suggesting that the lower courts had seriously misappreciated it, leading to a grave injustice that warranted the Supreme Court's intervention.
respondent_arguments: The respondent implicitly argued that the Court should not reappreciate the evidence, as there were no exceptional or special circumstances, nor was there any substantial and grave injustice to justify departing from the concurrent findings of the trial court and the High Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants was justified when it was based on the sole testimony of a single witness (P.W. 9), especially after the High Court had disbelieved other corroborating witnesses.
appellant_arguments: The conviction was not justified because it was based on the sole testimony of P.W. 9.
The testimony of P.W. 9 is unreliable because the High Court disbelieved the other witnesses (P.Ws. 1 and 2) who were meant to corroborate his statement.
The presence of minor contradictions and embellishments in P.W. 9's statement further detracts from its value.
respondent_arguments: The testimony of the single witness, P.W. 9, was credible and sufficient for conviction, as he was the injured witness.
P.W. 9's testimony was reliable because the incident occurred in daylight, the appellants were well-known to him, and he had no motive to falsely implicate them.
His version was corroborated by medical evidence and by the fact that he named the appellants as his assailants at the earliest opportunity.
The fact that the High Court disbelieved other witnesses does not invalidate the credible testimony of the main injured witness.
Both the trial court and the High Court had concurrently accepted P.W. 9's testimony.

cases.case_name: Hem Raj v. The State of Ajmer
cases.principle: The Supreme Court does not exercise its over-riding powers under Art. 136(1) of the Constitution to re-appraise evidence unless it is shown that exceptional and special circumstances exist, that substantial and grave injustice has been done, and the case presents features of sufficient gravity to warrant a review. The fact that an appeal has been admitted by special leave does not entitle the appellant to open the whole case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court will not ordinarily reappreciate evidence unless exceptional and special circumstances exist, which are established when a serious misappreciation of evidence by lower courts has resulted in substantial and grave injustice. Even when special leave to appeal is granted, only those points that were fit to be urged at the preliminary stage can be argued at the final hearing.
obiter: The conviction of an appellant on the sole testimony of an injured witness can be justified if that testimony is corroborated by medical evidence and the witness is otherwise found to be credible, even if other witnesses who tried to corroborate the testimony were disbelieved by the High Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The conviction of the appellants was justified based on the sole testimony of the injured witness (P.W. 9), whose evidence was found to be credible, probable, and corroborated by medical evidence. The Supreme Court declined to reappreciate the evidence as there were no exceptional circumstances or grave injustice to warrant interference with the concurrent findings of the trial court and the High Court.
legal_tests_applied: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court will not ordinarily reappreciate evidence unless it is satisfied that exceptional and special circumstances exist, and that a substantial and grave injustice has been done as a result of a serious misappreciation of evidence by the lower courts.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants failed to demonstrate that exceptional circumstances or a grave injustice existed, which is the required threshold for the Supreme Court to reappreciate evidence and overturn concurrent findings of fact from lower courts.

The argument that P.W. 9's testimony was unreliable was rejected because the court found that the High Court's disbelief of other corroborating witnesses did not invalidate the core testimony of the main injured witness.
The court determined that the presence of 'certain minor contradictions and embellishments' in P.W. 9's statement was not significant enough to 'detract from the value of his testimony.'
why_respondent_won: The testimony of the single witness, P.W. 9, was deemed sufficient for conviction because he was the injured witness and his testimony was found to be credible by both the trial court and the High Court.

P.W. 9's testimony was considered reliable because the incident occurred in daylight, the appellants were well-known to him (preventing misidentification), and he had no motive to falsely implicate them.

The witness's account was corroborated by objective evidence, specifically the medical evidence of his injuries and the fact that he named the appellants as his assailants at the earliest possible opportunity.
The court upheld the principle that it should not interfere with concurrent findings of fact by lower courts in the absence of a compelling reason, such as grave injustice.
policy_considerations: The Supreme Court's power under Article 136 is an 'over-riding' and extraordinary jurisdiction, not a routine right of appeal. The Court restrains itself from exercising this power to open up the whole case and contest all findings of fact, preserving the finality of lower court decisions unless a grave injustice has occurred.
